description: Resources versus reserves, the uses of key minerals, and prospecting techniques.
content_html:
Resources and Reserves: An Important Distinction

Geologists draw a sharp distinction between two terms that students often confuse. A resource is any natural deposit that could potentially be of use — whether or not it is economical to extract today. A reserve is the part of that resource that can actually be extracted profitably right now. The difference matters enormously: a uranium deposit deep beneath the Antarctic ice sheet is a resource but not a reserve — current technology and cost make extraction impractical. If extraction costs fall or the uranium price rises, it may become a reserve.

This dynamic relationship means that reserves are not fixed: they change as commodity prices, technology and environmental regulations evolve. Understanding this distinction is also central to debate about how long mineral supplies will last and how geologists prioritise the search for new deposits.

Key Minerals and Their Uses

Minerals extracted from the Earth serve three broad economic sectors: construction, industrial manufacturing, and energy generation. Limestone aggregate is quarried at enormous scale — in the UK, the Carboniferous Limestone of the Pennines and the Mendip Hills produces millions of tonnes annually for road base, concrete and cement. Sand and gravel from glacial and fluvial deposits are equally important for the construction industry.

For industrial manufacturing, metallic minerals are paramount. Ore minerals include haematite (Fe₂O₃) and magnetite (Fe₃O₄), both iron ores central to steel production. Galena (PbS) is the principal ore of lead; sphalerite (ZnS) is the primary zinc ore; chalcopyrite (CuFeS₂) is the most common copper-bearing mineral. These ore minerals typically occur in veins — mineral-filled fractures deposited by hot hydrothermal fluids passing through the host rock — or in disseminated deposits spread through large volumes of rock.

For energy generation, uranium (occurring in pitchblende/uraninite, UO₂) is extracted for nuclear fuel. Uranium occurs in sandstone-hosted roll-front deposits and in igneous and metamorphic basement rocks. Coal, extracted from Carboniferous sedimentary sequences across the UK and globally, remains an important resource despite pressure from renewable energy.

Key Fact

Key ore minerals to know: haematite (Fe₂O₃) — iron; magnetite (Fe₃O₄) — iron; chalcopyrite (CuFeS₂) — copper; galena (PbS) — lead; sphalerite (ZnS) — zinc. These are the spec-listed ore minerals. Using an alternative mineral name that is not on the spec will cost marks.

Finding New Deposits: Prospecting Techniques

Modern mineral prospecting uses a staged approach, beginning with low-cost wide-area surveys and narrowing to targeted, expensive investigation of promising zones.

Geological mapping is always the first step. Surface geology maps compiled by the British Geological Survey (BGS) and its international equivalents identify rock types, faults and structural features that control where ore deposits might be located. Borehole correlation — comparing the rock sequences encountered in multiple boreholes — extends this understanding into the subsurface and uses microfossils (foraminifera, pollen, spores) to correlate strata between holes where physical tracing is impossible.

Geophysical prospecting covers several techniques. Seismic surveys send acoustic waves into the ground and record the reflections from subsurface boundaries, revealing structures such as anticlines or faults that may trap oil and gas. Magnetic surveys detect contrasts in the magnetic properties of rocks; mineral-rich bodies such as magnetite ore or kimberlite pipes often show distinctive magnetic anomalies. Ground-penetrating radar (GPR) uses high-frequency radio waves to image shallow features (typically the top 10–30 m) and is useful for mapping sand and gravel deposits.

Geochemical surveys analyse the chemistry of soils and river sediments to detect elevated concentrations of metals that indicate an ore body nearby. Plants growing over a copper deposit, for example, may have anomalously high copper in their tissue. River sediment surveys sample stream beds downstream from mineralised zones: because erosion continuously supplies material from upstream, the chemical composition of sediment reflects what lies uphill. This approach can quickly screen thousands of square kilometres with a relatively small team. Anomalies flagged by geochemical surveys are then prioritised for more expensive borehole drilling.

Key Fact

Prospecting moves from cheap, wide-area methods to expensive, targeted ones: geological mapping → geophysical surveys (seismic, magnetic, GPR) → geochemical surveys (soil, river sediment) → borehole drilling. Each stage reduces the search area for the next, controlling costs.

When a target zone has been identified by surface surveys, boreholes are drilled to retrieve core samples. Geologists log each core — describing rock type, colour, grain size, fossil content and any mineralisation. Cores from multiple boreholes can be correlated by matching distinctive horizons, marker beds, or assemblages of microfossils. Foraminifera (marine microfossils) and pollen or spores (continental microfossils) have short stratigraphic ranges, making them precise time markers across a basin. Borehole correlation builds a three-dimensional picture of the subsurface that guides decisions about where to drill production wells or mine shafts.
exam_tip_html: Do not confuse resources and reserves in your answers — this is a heavily tested distinction. A resource is any known deposit; a reserve is the economically extractable part. Remember too that only spec-listed mineral names gain marks: haematite, magnetite, chalcopyrite, galena, sphalerite. Using “iron ore” without the mineral name, or naming a mineral not on the spec, will cost you. For “describe” questions on prospecting techniques, name the technique, describe what it measures and say what feature it helps detect — that's usually 2 marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A resource is any known deposit of useful material; a reserve is the economically extractable portion. Reserves change as prices, technology and regulations change.
  • Key ore minerals include haematite and magnetite (iron), chalcopyrite (copper), galena (lead) and sphalerite (zinc) — learn these names and chemical formulae exactly as they appear on the spec.
  • Prospecting uses a staged approach from low-cost geological and geochemical surveys to expensive borehole drilling, progressively narrowing the search area for new mineral deposits.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct ore mineral for copper?
A) Galena (PbS)
B) Sphalerite (ZnS)
C) Chalcopyrite (CuFeS₂)
D) Haematite (Fe₂O₃)
Name the type of survey that analyses the chemistry of soils and river sediments to locate mineral deposits.
Describe the difference between a mineral resource and a mineral reserve.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for:
- A mineral resource is a known natural deposit that may be useful, whether or not it can currently be extracted profitably. (1)
- A mineral reserve is the part of a resource that has been identified and can be extracted at a profit using current technology and economic conditions. (1)

practice_questions.text: A geochemical survey samples river sediment at three points downstream of a mineralised hillside. The copper concentration at station A (nearest the hill) is 480 ppm, at station B it is 240 ppm, and at station C it is 120 ppm. What is the percentage decrease in copper concentration between station A and station C? Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Percentage decrease = ((480 - 120) / 480) × 100 = (360 / 480) × 100 = 75%
[2 marks: 1 for correct method, 1 for correct answer]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a magnetic survey can help locate a mineral deposit in the subsurface.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- Magnetic surveys measure variations in the strength of the Earth's magnetic field across a survey area, using sensitive instruments called magnetometers. (1)
- Rocks with high iron content (such as magnetite ore bodies) produce a distinctive positive magnetic anomaly — a local increase in field strength above the regional background. (1)
- By mapping these anomalies, geologists can identify the location, approximate shape and depth of a buried magnetic ore body, guiding the siting of boreholes to confirm the find. (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the staged approach to mineral prospecting. Consider the advantages of moving from geological mapping through geophysical and geochemical surveys to borehole drilling, and discuss any limitations of this approach.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear understanding of the cost-reduction logic behind staging; evaluates both advantages and limitations with specific examples of techniques; reaches a reasoned conclusion about overall effectiveness.
Secure: Discusses at least three stages with advantages identified; limitations mentioned but may be less developed; conclusion present.
Developing: Describes the stages adequately but evaluation is limited; limitations may be absent.
Emerging: Names one or two techniques without structured evaluation.

Advantages:
- Starting with low-cost methods (geological mapping, geochemical surveys) screens out unpromising areas cheaply before expensive drilling is committed.
- Seismic surveys can image deep subsurface structures invisible at the surface, identifying traps or anticlinal features that control ore and hydrocarbon distribution.
- Geochemical anomalies in river sediment rapidly identify mineralised catchments across large areas with a small field team, providing cost-effective first-pass screening.
- Borehole core provides definitive confirmation of ore type, grade and geometry before capital-intensive mining begins.

Limitations:
- Each technique has a depth limitation: GPR is effective only to ~30 m; surface geochemical surveys reflect shallow weathering zones and may miss deep ore bodies.
- Geophysical surveys require interpretation expertise; anomalies may reflect unmineralised rock types (e.g. magnetic anomaly from mafic intrusion rather than ore).
- Drilling is expensive and samples only a tiny fraction of the subsurface volume; interpolation between holes always carries uncertainty.
- The approach assumes ore is detectable from the surface — some deeply buried or weakly mineralised deposits escape detection at all stages.

Conclusion: The staged approach is economically rational and technically well-founded; it concentrates expensive investment in the areas most likely to be productive. However, it is not infallible — the depth of each technique limits what can be detected, and exploration always involves geological uncertainty. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a resource and a reserve?
options: A resource can always be extracted profitably; a reserve may not be
A reserve is the economically extractable part of a resource
Resources and reserves are the same thing
A reserve is discovered by geochemical surveys; a resource by geological mapping

Seismic surveys send _____ waves into the ground and record reflections from subsurface boundaries to reveal underground structures.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a mineral resource and a mineral reserve?
flashcard_questions.a: Resource: any known useful deposit. Reserve: the portion currently extractable at a profit.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the ore mineral for iron (two acceptable answers)?
What is the ore mineral for copper?
What is the ore mineral for lead?
What is the ore mineral for zinc?
Why do mineral reserves change over time even if no new deposits are found?
flashcard_questions.a: Changing commodity prices or technology may make previously uneconomic deposits profitable to extract.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a magnetic survey detect in mineral prospecting?
flashcard_questions.a: Variations in the Earth's magnetic field caused by iron-rich ore bodies such as magnetite.

flashcard_questions.q: What does ground-penetrating radar (GPR) image in prospecting?
flashcard_questions.a: Shallow subsurface features (typically the top 10–30 m) including sand and gravel deposits.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do prospectors sample river sediment downstream of a hillside?
flashcard_questions.a: Erosion continuously supplies material from upstream, so sediment chemistry reflects what lies uphill.

flashcard_questions.q: What are microfossils used for in borehole correlation?
flashcard_questions.a: To match rock horizons between boreholes by identifying the same fossil assemblage in each.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the first stage of the staged prospecting approach and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Geological mapping — it is cheap and identifies rock types and structures controlling ore locations.

glossary_terms.definition: A naturally occurring deposit of a material that may be useful to humans, whether or not it can currently be extracted profitably.
The part of a resource that has been identified, measured, and can currently be extracted at a profit using existing technology and economic conditions.
A naturally occurring mineral from which a metal can be profitably extracted; examples include haematite (iron), chalcopyrite (copper) and galena (lead).
Prospecting methods that measure physical properties of rocks from the surface or from aircraft, including seismic surveys, magnetic surveys and ground-penetrating radar.
